# ShopSense AI: Exploratory Data Analysis Summary

**Dataset:** UCI Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention Dataset (ID 468), `online_shoppers_intention.csv`
**Generated by:** `python -m ml.eda` (figures in `figures/`, numbers in `tables/` and `eda_stats.json`)
**Scope:** Descriptive analysis of the full dataset. No model was trained and no preprocessing was fitted.
Every number below comes from `eda_stats.json`. Associations are not causal effects.

---

## 1. Dataset overview

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Rows (sessions) | 12,330 |
| Columns | 18 (17 features + target `Revenue`) |
| Missing values | 0 in every column |
| Exact duplicate rows | 125 (1.0%) |
| Purchases (`Revenue = True`) | 1,908 (15.47%) |
| No purchase (`Revenue = False`) | 10,422 (84.53%) |
| Months present | Feb, Mar, May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep, Oct, Nov, Dec (no Jan or Apr) |
| Original file integrity | SHA-256 matches the downloaded file before and after EDA |

**Feature groups**
- *Numeric (10):* Administrative, Administrative_Duration, Informational, Informational_Duration,
  ProductRelated, ProductRelated_Duration, BounceRates, ExitRates, PageValues, SpecialDay
- *Categorical (6):* Month, VisitorType, plus four integer-coded categoricals
  (OperatingSystems, Browser, Region, TrafficType). These codes have no numeric order.
- *Boolean (1):* Weekend

### Data quality notes
- **Duplicates:** All 125 duplicate rows are non-purchase sessions with zero duration on every page type
  and bounce and exit rates of 0.2 (single-page bounces). They are plausibly separate real sessions with
  identical values, so they are **kept by default**. `clean(drop_duplicates=True)` removes them if
  needed.
- **Label format:** June is stored as `June` while all other months are 3-letter abbreviations.
  `clean()` normalises it to `Jun`.
- **Zero durations:** 717 sessions visited at least one product page but have a product-page duration
  of 0. 755 sessions in total have zero product-page duration. In Google Analytics a page's time is
  recorded only when another page follows it, which may explain this. Treat zero durations with care.
- **Rate ceiling:** BounceRates and ExitRates both peak at 0.2. 700 sessions sit exactly at the 0.2
  bounce-rate ceiling.
- 6 sessions record zero pages of any type.

---

## 2. Key findings

### 2.1 The target is imbalanced: 15.5% conversion
*Figure: `figures/01_conversion_rate.png`*

1,908 of 12,330 sessions ended in a purchase, about 5.5 non-purchases per purchase. A model that
always predicts "no purchase" would be 84.5% accurate, so **accuracy is not a useful metric** for the
modelling phase. Use stratified splits and imbalance-aware metrics (precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC,
ROC-AUC).

### 2.2 New visitors convert at a higher rate than returning visitors
*Figure: `figures/02_visitor_type.png`*

| Visitor type | Sessions | Share | Conversion | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Returning_Visitor | 10,551 | 85.6% | 13.9% | 13.3–14.6% |
| New_Visitor | 1,694 | 13.7% | 24.9% | 22.9–27.0% |
| Other | 85 | 0.7% | 18.8% | 11.9–28.4% |

- The difference is statistically significant (χ² = 135.3, df = 2, p ≈ 4×10⁻³⁰), but the
  association is weak (Cramér's V = 0.10).
- Returning visitors make up most of the traffic and therefore most purchases (1,470 of 1,908), even
  though their conversion rate is lower.
- "Other" has only 85 sessions, so its rate is uncertain (wide interval).
- New visitors spend *less* time on product pages (median 414 s vs 656 s for returning visitors), so
  their higher conversion is not explained by browsing time.

### 2.3 Longer product-page browsing goes with higher conversion
*Figure: `figures/03_product_page_duration.png`*

- Median product-page time: **18.5 min (1,110 s) for purchasers** vs **8.5 min (510 s) for
  non-purchasers**. Means: 1,876 s vs 1,070 s.
- Mann-Whitney U: p < 0.001. Rank-biserial correlation 0.35, a moderate effect.
- Conversion rises steadily across equal-size duration groups:

| Duration quintile | 0–2 min | 2–7 min | 7–14 min | 14–30 min | 30+ min |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Conversion | 4.1% | 9.4% | 17.6% | 21.0% | 25.3% |

- Durations are strongly right-skewed (max ≈ 63,974 s). The preprocessing pipeline applies `log1p`
  before scaling.

### 2.4 Bounce rate: purchasers almost never bounce heavily
*Figure: `figures/04_bounce_rate.png`*

- Median bounce rate: **0.00% for purchasers** vs **0.43% for non-purchasers** (means 0.51% vs
  2.53%). Mann-Whitney p < 0.001. Rank-biserial −0.23, a weak-to-moderate effect.
- Conversion falls sharply above about 1% bounce rate: 12.9% (1–2%), 6.5% (2–5%), 2.6% (5–10%) and
  **0.5% (10–20%, 4 purchases in 816 sessions)**.
- The relationship is **not monotonic at the low end**. Sessions with exactly 0% bounce convert at
  18.8%, below the 0–0.5% band at 24.8%. Treat BounceRates as non-linear.

### 2.5 Exit rate separates the classes more clearly than bounce rate
*Figure: `figures/05_exit_rate.png`*

- Median exit rate: **1.60% for purchasers** vs **2.86% for non-purchasers** (means 1.96% vs 4.74%).
  Rank-biserial −0.41, a moderate effect and stronger than bounce rate.
- Conversion falls across the exit-rate bands, from 27.7% (0–0.5%) to 13.4% (2–5%), 4.3% (5–10%) and
  **0.5% (10–20%)**. The 0% band (44.7%) has only 76 sessions and a wide interval (34–56%).
- ExitRates and BounceRates are correlated (Spearman ρ = 0.60), so they carry partly overlapping
  information.

### 2.6 Monthly trends: November dominates purchases
*Figure: `figures/06_monthly_trends.png`*

| Month | Sessions | Purchases | Conversion |
|---|---|---|---|
| Feb | 184 | 3 | 1.6% |
| Mar | 1,907 | 192 | 10.1% |
| May | 3,364 | 365 | 10.9% |
| Jun | 288 | 29 | 10.1% |
| Jul | 432 | 66 | 15.3% |
| Aug | 433 | 76 | 17.6% |
| Sep | 448 | 86 | 19.2% |
| Oct | 549 | 115 | 20.9% |
| **Nov** | **2,998** | **760** | **25.4%** |
| Dec | 1,727 | 216 | 12.5% |

- **May has the most sessions (3,364)**, but **November has the highest conversion (25.4%)** and
  accounts for **39.8% of all purchases** (760 of 1,908).
- Conversion rises steadily from July to November, then drops in December (12.5%).
- February has very few sessions (184) and the lowest conversion (1.6%, 3 purchases).
- Month and conversion are associated (χ² = 384.9, df = 9, p ≈ 2×10⁻⁷⁷, Cramér's V = 0.18).
- **Caveat:** There is no year field and January and April are absent, so this shows seasonality
  within one sampled period, not a multi-year trend. Session counts vary greatly by month, so
  low-traffic months have wide intervals.

### 2.7 PageValues has by far the strongest association with purchase
*Figure: `figures/07_correlation_heatmap.png`*

- Spearman ρ with Revenue: **PageValues 0.63**. The next strongest are ExitRates −0.25,
  ProductRelated_Duration 0.22 and ProductRelated 0.20. All others are below 0.17 in absolute value.
- 80.6% of purchasing sessions have PageValues > 0, compared with 11.4% of non-purchasing sessions.
- Conversion is **56.3% when PageValues > 0** (2,730 sessions) vs **3.9% when it is 0** (9,600
  sessions). Rank-biserial 0.73, a large effect.
- The page-count and duration pairs are highly correlated (Administrative ↔ duration 0.94,
  Informational ↔ duration 0.95, ProductRelated ↔ duration 0.88), so they are largely redundant.

### 2.8 Secondary observations
- **Weekend:** 17.4% conversion vs 14.9% on weekdays. The difference is significant (p = 0.001) but
  the association is very weak (Cramér's V = 0.03).
- **SpecialDay:** Sessions near a special day (SpecialDay > 0, n = 1,251) convert at 6.2%, vs
  16.5% otherwise. However, SpecialDay > 0 occurs **only in February and May**, so it is confounded
  with month. Within May alone it is 6.4% (SpecialDay > 0) vs 13.2% (SpecialDay = 0).

---

## 3. Implications for modelling (Phase 3)

1. **Class imbalance:** Use stratified train/test splitting (already done by `make_train_test_split`)
   and imbalance-aware metrics. Consider class weights.
2. **PageValues leakage check:** The UCI documentation describes PageValues as the average value of
   pages a user visited *before completing an e-commerce transaction*. Its very strong separation of
   the classes is consistent with it partly encoding the outcome itself. Train and compare models
   **with and without** PageValues (`build_preprocessor(exclude=("PageValues",))`) before relying on
   it, especially for a real-time prediction use case.
3. **Skewed features:** Counts, durations and PageValues are heavily right-skewed. The pipeline
   applies `log1p` and then standard scaling. Tree-based models do not need this.
4. **Redundancy:** Count and duration pairs are highly correlated, which matters for linear-model
   coefficients and SHAP attributions. Expect importance to be shared between them.
5. **Categoricals:** Month, VisitorType and the four integer-coded features are one-hot encoded with
   `handle_unknown="ignore"`, so January and April (never seen) are handled safely at inference time.
6. **Non-linear effects:** BounceRates and the 0% exit band are non-monotonic, which favours flexible
   models (e.g. gradient boosting or random forests) or binned features.

---

## 4. Leakage safeguards in this phase
- The original CSV is read-only in code. Its SHA-256 is recorded at download and checked by
  `load_raw()`, and it was confirmed unchanged after EDA.
- `clean()` applies only stateless, row-level fixes (label normalisation, type casting).
- Imputation, scaling and one-hot encoding live in an **unfitted** `ColumnTransformer`, to be fitted on
  the training split only.
- The EDA uses the full dataset **for description only**. The quantile bins and bands in the charts
  are for presentation and are not model features.
- `Revenue` is never included in the feature set.

## 5. Reproduce

```powershell
cd backend
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -I ml/download_data.py    # skips if the CSV is already present
python -m ml.data_preprocessing  # validation + train/test split preview
python -m ml.eda                 # regenerates figures/, tables/, eda_stats.json
```
